content: The atrium, or atria in plural, refers to a chamber or cavity within the body. In the context of the heart, it is a thin-walled structure that collects blood returning to the heart. Animals with closed circulatory systems have at least one atrium. In fish, the heart is two-chambered, consisting of one atrium and one ventricle. In other vertebrates, the heart is either three-chambered, with two atria and one ventricle, or four-chambered, with two atria and two ventricles. The atrium functions to receive blood returning to the heart, while the ventricle pumps blood out of the heart to initiate a new circulatory cycle. Humans have a four-chambered heart, which includes the right atrium, left atrium, right ventricle, and left ventricle. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the superior and inferior vena cava and sends it to the right ventricle, which pumps it to the lungs for oxygenation. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins and pumps it to the left ventricle, which then sends it to the aorta for systemic circulation. The atria lack valves at their inlets, which allows for normal venous pulsations that can be observed in the jugular vein. Internally, the atria contain structures such as the musculae pectinati, the crista terminalis (a boundary within the atrium), and the smooth-walled region derived from the sinus venosus. Additionally, the interatrial septum contains the fossa ovalis, a remnant of the fetal foramen ovale that bypassed the lungs during development. Anatomy of the Right Atrium The right atrium forms the right border of the heart. The superior vena cava and inferior vena cava drain systemic venous blood into the smooth posterior wall of the right atrium. The anterior wall of the right atrium is ridged and composed of pectinate muscles, which form a rough muscular surface. Right Auricle The right auricle is a conical, ear-like muscular pouch that overlaps the ascending aorta. It is an embryonic remnant that increases the capacity of the right atrium. Openings of the Superior and Inferior Vena Cava The superior vena cava opens into the superior part of the right atrium at the level of the right third costal cartilage. The inferior vena cava opens into the inferior part of the right atrium, nearly in line with the superior vena cava, at the level of the fifth costal cartilage. Coronary Sinus The coronary sinus is a venous structure that collects systemic blood from the cardiac veins and empties it into the posterior part of the right atrium. It is derived from the embryonic venous sinus. The opening of the coronary sinus is located between the right atrioventricular orifice and the inferior vena cava orifice. Sinus Venarum The sinus venarum is a smooth-walled posterior pouch in the right atrium where the superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, and coronary sinus deliver deoxygenated blood. It is formed by the incorporation of the embryonic venous sinus into the primordial atrium. The sinus venarum is separated from the primordial atrium by the sulcus terminalis externally and the crista terminalis internally. Fossa Ovalis The fossa ovalis is a depression in the interatrial septum, representing the remnant of the fetal foramen ovale. This structure allowed oxygenated blood from the placenta to bypass the lungs and flow directly from the right atrium to the left atrium during fetal development. The limbus of the fossa ovalis, or annulus ovalis, is the prominent margin surrounding the fossa ovalis. Anatomy of the Left Atrium The left atrium constitutes the majority of the heart's base. Its wall is slightly thicker than that of the right atrium, and the interatrial septum forms part of its posterior and rightward wall. The interior of the left atrium consists of two main regions: a larger smooth-walled portion, which is thought to develop from the absorption of embryonic pulmonary veins, and a smaller muscular auricle containing pectinate muscles, which is a remnant of the left part of the primordial atrium. Pulmonary Veins The left atrium receives oxygenated blood through four valveless pulmonary veins, which are arranged in two pairs (left and right) and open into its posterior wall. Left Auricle The left auricle is a small muscular pouch that overlaps the pulmonary trunk and forms the superior part of the left border of the heart. It contains pectinate muscles within its walls, similar to the right auricle. Left Atrioventricular Orifice The left atrioventricular orifice is the site where oxygenated blood exits the left atrium and flows into the left ventricle. This blood is then pumped into the aorta for systemic distribution.
